Exercise 1 uses a laboratory experiment on the survival of tadpoles, Exercises 2 and 3 use
field counts of glacier lily seedlings, and Exercise 4 uses measurements of trees that come
with R. Exercise 5 simulates hypothetical samples from the model fitted in Exercise 4. Exercises 1 to 4 are the core of the practical and Exercise 5 is extra
practice. The data of Exercises 1 to 3 are in the package `emdbook`. Work through the first
example before trying the remaining exercises. The ideas and notation are introduced in the
[Chapter 4 theory](../Theory.qmd).

As in the theory, every model is written and fitted with the packages RTMB and RTMBdist,
which you installed in the Chapter 1 practical together with `emdbook`. Load RTMB first and
RTMBdist second:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)
```

# Exercise 1: Survival of reed frog tadpoles

The data set `ReedfrogPred` in the package `emdbook` contains the results of laboratory
experiments on the predation of tadpoles of the African reed frog *Hyperolius spinigularis*
(Vonesh and Bolker 2005). Each row is a tank of 1.2 × 0.8 × 0.4 m. The variable `density`
is the number of tadpoles that were placed in the tank at the start (10, 25 or 35) and
`surv` is the number of tadpoles that survived. Questions 1 to 5 use the 24 tanks with
predators, and question 6 also uses the 24 tanks without them:

```{r}
# Load the reed frog data from the emdbook package without attaching the package.
data(ReedfrogPred, package = "emdbook")

# Keep the 24 tanks with predators.
predator_tanks = ReedfrogPred[ReedfrogPred$pred == "pred", ]

# Initial number of tadpoles in each tank and number of survivors, and the number of tanks.
tadpoles = predator_tanks$density
survivors = predator_tanks$surv
n_tanks = length(survivors)
```

Let $X_i$ be the number of survivors in tank $i$, which started with $n_i$ tadpoles. We use
a [Binomial](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-binomial) model with the same
probability of survival $p$ in all the tanks,

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_i, p),
$$

and assume that the tanks are independent. Note that the tanks are not identically
distributed, because $n_i$ differs among them. The likelihood is still the product of the
contributions of the tanks, since the product only requires independence. Each contribution
is calculated with the $n_i$ of its own tank.

1. On paper, write the likelihood contributions of the first three tanks (4, 9 and 7
   survivors out of 10 tadpoles each) and their likelihood as a function of $p$. Calculate
   the likelihood and the log-likelihood for $p=0.5$ and for $p=2/3$, and verify the
   results in R.
2. On paper, derive the maximum likelihood estimator of $p$ for all the tanks by
   differentiating the log-likelihood (the
   [rules of differentiation](../../Supplements/calculus.qmd#sec-calc-rules) are in the
   calculus refresher). Calculate the estimate.
3. Write the negative log-likelihood (NLL) with $\operatorname{logit}p$ as the parameter,
   process it with `MakeADFun()` and minimise it with `optim()`. Check the convergence and
   report the estimate of $p$. Calculate the standard error of the estimate of
   $\operatorname{logit}p$ in two ways: from the Hessian that `optim()` returns with
   `hessian = TRUE`, and with `sdreport()`. Then calculate a 95% Wald interval for $p$, and
   the standard error of $\hat p$ itself with `ADREPORT()`.
4. Calculate the 95% likelihood interval for $p$ with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and
   `confint()`, and compare it with the Wald interval.
5. Is the Binomial model adequate for these data? For each initial density, compare the
   variance of the number of survivors among tanks with the variance of the fitted model.
   What does the comparison imply for the intervals of questions 3 and 4?
6. The experiment also had 24 tanks without predators. Fit a model with one probability of
   survival for all 48 tanks and a model with one probability for each treatment, and
   compare them with AIC and AICc. How much does the presence of predators change the
   probability of survival? Calculate the difference between the two probabilities with
   its standard error, and 95% Wald intervals for both probabilities and for their
   difference.

## Solution

### Question 1

The observational unit is one tank. The contribution of a tank to the likelihood is the
probability that the Binomial model assigns to its number of survivors,
$P(X_i=x_i\mid p)=\binom{n_i}{x_i}p^{x_i}(1-p)^{n_i-x_i}$. The first three tanks started
with 10 tadpoles each and had 4, 9 and 7 survivors, so their likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(p\mid 4,9,7)
&= \binom{10}{4}p^{4}(1-p)^{6}\times
   \binom{10}{9}p^{9}(1-p)^{1}\times
   \binom{10}{7}p^{7}(1-p)^{3}\\
&= 210\times 10\times 120\;p^{20}(1-p)^{10}
= 252{,}000\;p^{20}(1-p)^{10}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The exponents are the total number of survivors (20) and the total number of tadpoles that
died (10) in the three tanks. For $p=0.5$ the likelihood is
$252{,}000/2^{30}\approx 2.35\times10^{-4}$ and for $p=2/3$ it is
$252{,}000\times 2^{20}/3^{30}\approx 1.28\times10^{-3}$. The log-likelihood is the
logarithm of the same expression,

$$
\ell(p)=\log(252{,}000)+20\log p+10\log(1-p),
$$

which gives $12.437-20.794=-8.357$ for $p=0.5$ and $12.437-8.109-10.986=-6.658$ for
$p=2/3$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# The first three tanks: survivors and initial number of tadpoles.
first_survivors = survivors[1:3]
first_tadpoles = tadpoles[1:3]
first_survivors
first_tadpoles

# Likelihood contribution of each tank at p = 0.5 and at p = 2/3, and the likelihood of the
# three tanks, which is the product of the contributions.
dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 0.5)
dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 2 / 3)
prod(dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 0.5))
prod(dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 2 / 3))

# Log-likelihood at the same two values: the sum of the log probabilities.
sum(dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 0.5, log = TRUE))
sum(dbinom(x = first_survivors, size = first_tadpoles, prob = 2 / 3, log = TRUE))
```

R returns the same values. The difference between the two log-likelihoods is 1.70, so the
three counts are about 5.5 times more probable ($e^{1.70}$) under $p=2/3$ than under
$p=0.5$. This is no coincidence, as 20 of the 30 tadpoles in these three tanks survived.

### Question 2

For all the tanks the log-likelihood is the sum of the logarithms of the 24 contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell(p)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{24}\log\binom{n_i}{x_i}
 +\log(p)\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_i
 +\log(1-p)\sum_{i=1}^{24}(n_i-x_i),\\
\frac{d\ell}{dp}
&= \frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_i-\frac{1}{1-p}\sum_{i=1}^{24}(n_i-x_i),\\
0 &= \frac{1}{\hat p}\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_i-\frac{1}{1-\hat p}\sum_{i=1}^{24}(n_i-x_i)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat p=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{24}n_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first term of the log-likelihood does not contain $p$, so it disappears when we
differentiate. To solve the last line, multiply both sides by $\hat p(1-\hat p)$, which
gives $(1-\hat p)\sum x_i=\hat p\sum(n_i-x_i)$, and collect the terms with $\hat p$. The
second derivative, $-\sum x_i/p^2-\sum(n_i-x_i)/(1-p)^2$, is negative for every $p$, so
this is a maximum. In R:

```{r}
# Total number of survivors and of tadpoles, and the maximum likelihood estimate from
# the derivation: p_hat = sum(x_i) / sum(n_i).
total_survivors = sum(survivors)
total_tadpoles = sum(tadpoles)
p_hat = total_survivors / total_tadpoles
c(survivors = total_survivors, tadpoles = total_tadpoles, p_hat = p_hat)
```

In total 264 of the 560 tadpoles survived, so $\hat p=264/560\approx 0.471$. The maximum
likelihood estimator
(MLE) is the fraction of all the tadpoles that survived. That is, the tanks are pooled, and
a tank with 35 tadpoles weighs more in the estimate than a tank with 10.

### Question 3

A probability lies between zero and one, so we let the optimiser search over
$\operatorname{logit}p$, which can take any real value, and convert it into a probability
with `plogis()` inside the function. The NLL has the form of the theory: its first argument
is a list of parameters, with one element (`logit_p`), and its second argument a list of
data, with two elements (`survivors` and `tadpoles`). `dbinom()` receives the vector with
the initial number of tadpoles of each tank in its argument `size`. The line `ADREPORT(p)`
asks for the standard error of $p$ itself, which we use at the end of this question. We
connect the NLL to the data with `cmb()`, process it with `MakeADFun()` and start the
search at $p=0.5$, whose logit is zero:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Binomial model with one survival probability p for all tanks.
# The tanks differ in the number of tadpoles n_i, so size is a vector.
binomial_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # logit_p can take any real value and plogis() turns it into a probability.
  p = plogis(logit_p)
  # Ask for the standard error of p itself.
  ADREPORT(p)
  -sum(dbinom(x = survivors, size = tadpoles, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL of the 24 tanks, starting from p = 0.5 (logit 0).
frog_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, list(survivors = survivors, tadpoles = tadpoles)),
  list(logit_p = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)

# Fit with BFGS; hessian = TRUE is used for the standard error by hand.
frog_fit = optim(
  par = frog_obj$par,
  fn = frog_obj$fn,
  gr = frog_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE
)
frog_fit$convergence

# Estimate on the probability scale, and the minimum of the negative log-likelihood.
plogis(frog_fit$par)
frog_fit$value
```

The convergence code is 0. By invariance, `plogis()` of the estimate of
$\operatorname{logit}p$ is the MLE of $p$: 0.471, the value that we derived on paper. The
minimum of the NLL is 98.94, so the maximum log-likelihood is $-98.94$.

There are two routes to the standard error. The first is the calculation that the box on
the Hessian matrix in
[Curvature and standard errors](../Theory.qmd#sec-curvature) describes. The Hessian that
`optim()` returns refers to the parameter that it searched over, so its inverse is the
approximate variance of the estimate of $\operatorname{logit}p$:

```{r}
# The Hessian is a 1 by 1 matrix; take its single element.
frog_fit$hessian[1, 1]

# Standard error of the estimate of logit(p).
se_logit_p = sqrt(1 / frog_fit$hessian[1, 1])
se_logit_p
```

The second route is `sdreport()`, which does this calculation for any model and adds a row
for the quantity that we asked for with `ADREPORT()`. We calculate the Wald interval on
the logit scale and transform its endpoints back with `plogis()`:

```{r}
# Standard errors from sdreport(): the row logit_p is on the scale that was optimised and
# the row p is the quantity in ADREPORT().
frog_sd = sdreport(frog_obj)
frog_summary = summary(frog_sd)
frog_summary

# Wald interval on the logit scale, back-transformed to survival probabilities.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
wald_p = plogis(
  frog_summary["logit_p", "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * frog_summary["logit_p", "Std. Error"]
)
wald_p

# Standard error on the probability scale, from the formula for a proportion.
sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / total_tadpoles)
```

The Hessian is 139.5. By both routes the standard error of the estimate of $\operatorname{logit}p$ is
$1/\sqrt{139.5}\approx 0.085$, and the 95% Wald interval for the probability of survival
goes from 0.430 to 0.513. As in the theory, we transformed the endpoints and not the
standard error, because a standard error on the logit scale cannot be converted into a
probability with `plogis()`. The standard error of $\hat p$ itself is in the row `p` of
the table, 0.021: RTMB calculates it with the delta method (see the box on the delta
method in [Chapter 4](../../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained)). For this model we
can check it with a
formula: the observed information for $p$ is $\sum n_i/[\hat p(1-\hat p)]$, so the
standard error is $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/\sum n_i}\approx 0.021$.

### Question 4

The model has one parameter, so the profile is the log-likelihood itself. The likelihood
interval contains the values of $p$ whose relative log-likelihood is above the cutoff of
$-1.92$ (see [Likelihood profile intervals](../Theory.qmd#sec-profile_intervals)).
`TMB::tmbprofile()` calculates the profile of a parameter of the object, and `confint()`
finds the two values at which it crosses the cutoff. The profile is calculated on the logit
scale, so we transform the endpoints with `plogis()`:

```{r}
# Profile of logit(p) and the endpoints of its 95% interval, transformed back.
frog_profile = TMB::tmbprofile(frog_obj, name = "logit_p", trace = FALSE)
plogis(confint(frog_profile))
```

The likelihood interval goes from 0.430 to 0.513, the same as the Wald interval to three
decimals. The two methods agree because the sample is large: with 560 tadpoles the
log-likelihood is very close to a parabola on the logit scale, which is the approximation
behind the Wald interval. Under the Binomial model with independent tanks, we would report
that the probability of survival is 0.47 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.43 to 0.51.

### Question 5

The Binomial model gives the variance of the number of survivors, $n_ip(1-p)$, as well as
its mean, $n_ip$. The experiment has several tanks for each initial density, so we can
compare the variance of the number of survivors among the tanks of one density (calculated
with `var()`, which uses the divisor $n-1$) with the variance of the fitted model:

```{r}
# Variance of the number of survivors among tanks of the same initial density, and the
# variance that the Binomial model gives, n * p * (1 - p), with the estimated p.
densities = sort(unique(tadpoles))
variance_comparison = data.frame(
  density = densities,
  n_tanks = NA,
  observed_variance = NA,
  binomial_variance = NA
)
for (i in seq_along(densities)) {
  in_group = tadpoles == densities[i]
  variance_comparison$n_tanks[i] = sum(in_group)
  variance_comparison$observed_variance[i] = var(survivors[in_group])
  variance_comparison$binomial_variance[i] = densities[i] * p_hat * (1 - p_hat)
}
variance_comparison
```

There are eight tanks at each density. With 10 tadpoles the variance among tanks is 3.7,
against 2.5 under the model. With 25 tadpoles it is 24.8 against 6.2, and with 35 tadpoles
64.3 against 8.7. So the number of survivors varies more among tanks than the Binomial
model allows, up to seven times more: the counts are overdispersed relative to the Binomial
distribution (see [Chapter 2](../../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-discrete_distributions)). A
Binomial model with one $p$ assumes that every tadpole survives with the same probability
and independently of the others. Tadpoles in the same tank share their predators and their
conditions, so the probability of survival is likely to differ among tanks.

The consequence for questions 3 and 4 is that both intervals are too narrow. They are
calculated as if the model had generated the data, that is, as if we had 560 independent
tadpoles, while most of the variation is among the 24 tanks. The estimate of 0.47 is still
the overall fraction of survivors. A model in which $p$ varies among tanks is the
[Beta-Binomial](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-beta_binomial) distribution of the
supplement, and models for observations that are grouped are the subject of
[Chapter 7](../../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd), whose practical returns to these tanks with a
probability of survival that varies among them.

### Question 6

The two treatments belong to the same experiment, so we can compare them with a model for
all 48 tanks. The first model is the one of question 3 applied to all the tanks, with one
probability of survival ($K=1$). In the second model the tanks with predators have a
probability $p_{\mathrm{pred}}$ and the tanks without predators a probability
$p_{\mathrm{no}}$ ($K=2$), and the contribution of a tank is calculated with the
probability of its treatment. For the first model we connect `binomial_nll()` of question
3 to the 48 tanks: the list of data that we give to `cmb()` must use the names that the
NLL expects (`survivors` and `tadpoles`), whatever the objects are called in our session.
For the second model we write a new NLL in which `logit_p` is a vector with the logit of
the two probabilities, and the data include the number of the treatment of each tank
(`group`), which selects the probability of that tank. Both models are compared with AIC
and with AICc, which now uses the 48 tanks as $n$:

```{r}
# All 48 tanks: survivors, initial number of tadpoles and treatment ("no" or "pred").
survivors_all = ReedfrogPred$surv
tadpoles_all = ReedfrogPred$density
treatment = ReedfrogPred$pred
n_tanks_all = length(survivors_all)
table(treatment)

# Number of the treatment of each tank: as.numeric() of a factor returns the position of
# each level, so 1 is without predators ("no") and 2 with predators ("pred").
group = as.numeric(treatment)

# NLL of the model with one probability for each treatment. The first element of logit_p is
# the logit of the survival probability without predators and the second with predators.
treatment_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  p = plogis(logit_p)
  # Ask for the standard error of the difference between the two probabilities.
  difference = p[1] - p[2]
  ADREPORT(difference)
  # p[group] is the probability of the treatment of each tank.
  -sum(dbinom(x = survivors, size = tadpoles, prob = p[group], log = TRUE))
}

# Model with one probability: binomial_nll() of question 3 connected to the 48 tanks.
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(binomial_nll, list(survivors = survivors_all, tadpoles = tadpoles_all)),
  list(logit_p = 0),
  silent = TRUE
)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# Model with one probability for each treatment: the parameter is a vector of two logits.
treatment_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(
    treatment_nll,
    list(survivors = survivors_all, tadpoles = tadpoles_all, group = group)
  ),
  list(logit_p = c(0, 0)),
  silent = TRUE
)
treatment_fit = optim(
  par = treatment_obj$par,
  fn = treatment_obj$fn,
  gr = treatment_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
c(pooled = pooled_fit$convergence, treatment = treatment_fit$convergence)

# Estimates of the survival probabilities.
plogis(pooled_fit$par)
plogis(treatment_fit$par)

# AIC = 2K - 2 * log-likelihood and AICc = AIC + 2K(K + 1) / (n - K - 1), with K the
# number of parameters and n the number of tanks. The maximum log-likelihood is minus the
# minimum of the NLL.
n_parms = c(pooled = 1, treatment = 2)
loglik_tanks = c(pooled = -pooled_fit$value, treatment = -treatment_fit$value)
aic_tanks = 2 * n_parms - 2 * loglik_tanks
aicc_tanks = aic_tanks + 2 * n_parms * (n_parms + 1) / (n_tanks_all - n_parms - 1)
rbind(aic = aic_tanks, aicc = aicc_tanks)

# Standard errors: rows 1 and 2 are the logits of the probabilities without and with
# predators, and the row difference is the quantity in ADREPORT().
treatment_summary = summary(sdreport(treatment_obj))
treatment_summary

# 95% Wald intervals for the two probabilities: calculated on the logit scale, with the
# endpoints transformed back.
wald_no = plogis(
  treatment_summary[1, "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * treatment_summary[1, "Std. Error"]
)
wald_pred = plogis(
  treatment_summary[2, "Estimate"] +
    c(-1, 1) * critical_value * treatment_summary[2, "Std. Error"]
)
wald_no
wald_pred

# 95% Wald interval for the difference between the probabilities, on the original scale.
wald_difference = treatment_summary["difference", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * treatment_summary["difference", "Std. Error"]
wald_difference
```

Both fits have convergence code 0. The model with one probability estimates 0.699, the
fraction of the 1,120 tadpoles that survived. The model with two probabilities estimates
0.927 without predators and 0.471 with predators. These are the fractions of survivors in
each group of tanks, as the derivation of question 2 predicts for a Binomial model, and the
second is the estimate of question 3. The AIC is 574.5 for one probability and 274.3 for
one probability per treatment, and the AICc is 574.6 and 274.5. The difference of about
300 units is far larger than the two units that the additional parameter costs, and the
AICc gives the same comparison.

The ecological question is about the size of the effect. The probability of survival is
0.47 with predators (95% Wald interval from 0.43 to 0.51) and 0.93 without them (from 0.90
to 0.95), so the presence of predators lowers it by 0.46, from 0.93 to 0.47. The difference
is a quantity calculated from the two parameters, so we asked for it with `ADREPORT()`: its
standard error is 0.024, which gives a 95% Wald interval from 0.41 to 0.50.

The evidence is weaker than the difference in AIC suggests. Question 5 showed that the
counts of the tanks with predators vary more than the Binomial model allows, so their
interval is too narrow and the difference in AIC overstates the evidence. The direction
and the size of the effect are still what the data show. This is the first model of the
book in which a parameter differs between groups. In [Chapter 6](../../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd)
parameters will depend on continuous predictors, and in
[Chapter 7](../../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) on groups of observations.

# Exercise 2: Glacier lily seedlings in quadrats

The data set `Lily_sum` in the package `emdbook` contains counts of the glacier lily
*Erythronium grandiflorum* in a grid of 16 × 16 quadrats of 2 m × 2 m in Washington Gulch,
sampled in 1992 (Thomson et al. 1996). We use the column `seedlings`, the number of
seedlings in each of the 256 quadrats. Load the data with
`data(Lily_sum, package = "emdbook")`.

Let $X_i$ be the number of seedlings in quadrat $i$. We use a
[Negative Binomial](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial) model with
mean $\mu$ and shape $k$,

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{NegBin}(\mu, k), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{k},
$$

and assume that the quadrats are i.i.d. Neighbouring quadrats of a grid are likely to
resemble each other, so this is a simplification, as it was for the visits to owl nests in
the Chapter 3 practical. This course does not model the dependence among neighbouring
quadrats; [Chapter 7](../../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) deals with a related case, observations
that come in groups, such as the visits to one nest.

1. Estimate $\mu$ and $k$ with the method of moments, as in the Chapter 3 practical. Also
   calculate the fraction of quadrats without seedlings and the largest count.
2. Write the NLL of the model with $\log\mu$ and $\log k$ as parameters, process it with
   `MakeADFun()` and minimise it with `optim()`, using the method-of-moments estimates as
   starting values. Report the estimates on the original scale. Compare the log-likelihood
   at the maximum likelihood estimates with the log-likelihood at the method-of-moments
   estimates.
3. Calculate the log-likelihood on a grid of values of $\mu$ and $k$ (for example, $\mu$
   from 2.5 to 6 seedlings per quadrat and $k$ from 0.17 to 0.42) with two nested `for`
   loops that call the function `fn` of the object, and draw the contours of the relative
   log-likelihood with `contour()`. Add both pairs of estimates and the contour of the
   approximate joint 95% confidence region. Is the method-of-moments estimate inside the
   region?
4. Calculate a 95% Wald interval for $k$ (on the log scale, with the endpoints transformed
   back) with the standard error from `sdreport()`. Then calculate the 95% likelihood
   profile interval for $k$ with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()`, and compare it with
   the Wald interval.
5. Plot the relative frequencies of the counts together with the probabilities of the
   fitted Negative Binomial model and of a Poisson model fitted to the same counts (the
   maximum likelihood estimate of its mean is the sample mean). Compare the fraction of empty
   quadrats under each model with the observed fraction, and compare the two models with
   AIC and with its small-sample correction AICc (see
   [Model comparison with AIC](../Theory.qmd#sec-aic)).

# Exercise 3: Empty quadrats and zero inflation

About half of the quadrats of Exercise 2 have no seedlings. The Negative Binomial model
describes this with a small shape $k$. A different explanation is that a fraction of the
quadrats cannot have seedlings at all (for example, because no seeds arrive there), while
the counts in the rest follow a Poisson distribution. This is a zero-inflated Poisson
model (see
[How to make zero-inflated distributions](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-zero_inflated)
in the supplement). Its probability mass function is

$$
P(X=x\mid\lambda,p_0)=
\begin{cases}
p_0+(1-p_0)\,e^{-\lambda}, & x=0,\\[4pt]
(1-p_0)\,\dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x}}{x!}, & x>0,
\end{cases}
$$

where $p_0$ (`pzero` in the code of the supplement) is the probability that a quadrat
cannot have seedlings and $\lambda$ is the mean number of seedlings in the quadrats that
can have them. Use the same counts as in Exercise 2 and the same assumption of i.i.d.
quadrats.

1. Write a function `my_dzipois(x, lambda, pzero, log = FALSE)` that returns the
   probability mass of the zero-inflated Poisson distribution, or its logarithm when
   `log = TRUE`. Check that the probabilities add up to one over a wide range of counts,
   for two combinations of parameter values, and that your function returns the same
   probabilities as `dzipois()` of the package RTMBdist, in which $p_0$ is the argument
   `zeroprob`.
2. Write the NLL with `dzipois()` and with $\log\lambda$ and $\operatorname{logit}p_0$ as
   parameters. Choose starting values from the data (think of the fraction of empty
   quadrats and of the mean of the quadrats that are not empty) and fit the model.
   Interpret both estimates.
3. Compare the zero-inflated Poisson model with the Negative Binomial model of Exercise 2
   using AIC and AICc. What does the comparison come down to when both models have the
   same number of parameters?
4. Plot the probabilities of both fitted models over the relative frequencies of the
   counts. Under each model, calculate the probability of an empty quadrat and the
   probability of 20 or more seedlings, and compare them with the observed fractions. What
   does each model say about how the counts arise? Can the comparison identify the
   ecological cause of the empty quadrats?

# Exercise 4: Timber volume of black cherry trees

This exercise fits a model to continuous measurements, so the contributions to the
likelihood are densities. We use a [Gamma](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma)
model with shape $k$ and rate $r$ (`shape` and `rate` in R), for which

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(k, r), \qquad E[X_i]=\frac{k}{r},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\frac{k}{r^2}.
$$

We use the data set `trees` of the Chapter 3 practical, with the measurements of 31 felled
black cherry trees. That practical used their heights. Here $X_i$ is the volume of timber of
tree $i$ in cubic feet (ft³), the column `Volume`, and we assume that the trees are i.i.d.

1. Load the trees with `data(trees, package = "datasets")`. Write the NLL of the Gamma
   model with `dgamma(..., log = TRUE)` and with $\log k$ and $\log r$ as parameters, and
   mark the data with `OBS()`, which Exercise 5 uses to simulate. Exercise 5 also relies on
   these names: call the function `gamma_nll()`, the parameters `log_shape` and `log_rate`
   (in this order) and the data `x`. Calculate
   method-of-moments estimates from the formulas of the mean and the variance, use them as
   starting values and fit the model. Report the estimates of $k$ and $r$ with their units
   and the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean volume.
2. Calculate the correlation between the estimates of $\log k$ and $\log r$ with
   `sdreport()`. Calculate the log-likelihood on a grid of values of $k$ and $r$ (for
   example, $k$ from 1.5 to 8 and $r$ from 0.04 to 0.3/ft³) and draw the contours of the
   relative log-likelihood. What does the tilt of the contours mean?
3. Calculate a slice of the log-likelihood for the shape $k$, with the rate fixed at its
   estimate, on a grid of values, and the profile of $k$ with `TMB::tmbprofile()`, and plot
   both as relative log-likelihoods. Find the range of values of $k$ for which each curve
   is within 1.92 units of the maximum (for the profile, with `confint()`). Which of the two
   ranges is a confidence interval, and why is the slice narrower?

# Exercise 5: Estimators and intervals across hypothetical samples

This exercise is extra practice. With a single sample we cannot tell how far an estimate
is from the parameter, or whether a confidence interval contains it, because the parameter
is unknown. As in Exercise 3 of the Chapter 3 practical, we can study the behaviour of an
estimator by simulating hypothetical samples from a model whose parameters we know.
Here we use the maximum likelihood estimates of Exercise 4 as the parameters of that model.
The simulation then shows how the estimators and the intervals would behave if the fitted
Gamma model had generated the data (see
[Properties of maximum likelihood estimators](../Theory.qmd#sec-mle_properties) and
[Uncertainty from the likelihood](../Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty)). This
exercise continues with the objects of Exercise 4: `gamma_nll()`, the helper `cmb()` and
your estimates of the shape and the rate of the tree volumes.

Questions 1 and 2 each come with a chunk of code that is almost complete. Wherever the
code contains `NA`, replace the `NA` by your own code; the comment just above it says what
the code must calculate. Keep the names of the objects (`sim_obj`, `fit`, `lower`, ...),
because the lines that follow use them. The chunk will not run until every `NA` has been
replaced.

1. Simulate 2,000 hypothetical samples, each of 31 trees, from a Gamma model whose shape
   and rate are the maximum likelihood estimates of Exercise 4, and estimate the shape in
   each sample by the method of moments and by maximum likelihood. Complete and run the
   chunk below, which does this. Then calculate the mean, the standard deviation and the
   mean squared error of each estimator, and compare the means with the shape that you
   used to simulate.

The function `simulate_gamma_samples()` in the chunk draws every sample with the function
`simulate()` of an object that has placeholder data of the right length, as in the theory.
For each sample it calculates the method-of-moments estimate of the shape, fits the model
by maximum likelihood and stores the results in one row of the data frame `results`: the
two estimates of the shape (`shape_ml` and `shape_mom`), the standard error of the
estimate of $\log k$ from `sdreport()` (`se_log_shape`, which question 2 needs) and whether
the fit converged (`converged`). The sample size is an argument of the function because
question 3 uses another one. There are five `NA` to replace: three inside the loop, which
fit the model to one sample `x`, and two in the call at the end:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Simulate n_samples hypothetical samples of n_obs observations from a Gamma model with
# the given shape and rate, and estimate the shape in each of them.
simulate_gamma_samples = function(n_obs, shape, rate, n_samples) {
  # One row per sample; the loop replaces the zeros by the results.
  results = data.frame(
    shape_ml = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    shape_mom = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    se_log_shape = rep(0, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(FALSE, times = n_samples)
  )
  # An object with placeholder data of the right length, from which the samples are
  # simulated: the values of the data are not used.
  placeholder_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(gamma_nll, list(x = rep(0, times = n_obs))),
    list(log_shape = 0, log_rate = 0),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample (simulate() takes the parameters on the log scale).
    x = placeholder_obj$simulate(log(c(shape, rate)))$x

    # Method-of-moments estimate of the shape, from the mean and the variance (divisor n).
    x_mean = mean(x)
    x_variance = mean((x - x_mean)^2)
    shape_mom = x_mean^2 / x_variance

    # Replace NA: gamma_nll() connected to x with cmb() and processed with MakeADFun(),
    # with a shape of 1 and a rate of 1 / x_mean as starting values (on the log scale).
    sim_obj = NA
    # Replace NA: sim_obj minimised with optim() and method = "BFGS".
    fit = NA
    # Replace NA: the maximum likelihood estimate of the shape on the original scale.
    shape_ml = NA

    # Store the results of this sample.
    results$shape_ml[i] = shape_ml
    results$shape_mom[i] = shape_mom
    results$se_log_shape[i] = summary(sdreport(sim_obj))["log_shape", "Std. Error"]
    results$converged[i] = fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}

# 2,000 hypothetical samples of 31 trees. Replace each NA by your maximum likelihood
# estimate of the shape or of the rate from Exercise 4.
set.seed(seed = 801)
trees_31 = simulate_gamma_samples(n_obs = 31, shape = NA, rate = NA, n_samples = 2000)
```

2. For each sample, the 95% Wald interval for the shape is calculated as in Exercise 2: on
   the log scale, as the logarithm of the estimate plus or minus `critical_value` standard
   errors, with the endpoints transformed back with `exp()`. Complete and run the chunk
   below, which calculates the interval of every sample, checks whether it contains the
   shape that you used to simulate, and calculates the coverage of the interval. (The
   coverage of the likelihood profile interval would need `tmbprofile()` in every sample,
   which takes much longer, so we do not simulate it here.)

The chunk works with whole columns of `trees_31`: an operation on a column, such as
`log(trees_31$shape_ml)`, is applied to every sample at once, so no loop is needed.
`critical_value` is the 0.975 quantile of the standard Normal distribution,
`qnorm(p = 0.975)`, as in Exercise 1. There are three `NA` to replace:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace NA: the lower and the upper endpoint of the 95% Wald interval for the shape in
# every sample, from the columns shape_ml and se_log_shape of trees_31.
lower = NA
upper = NA
# Replace NA: TRUE for the samples whose interval contains the shape used to simulate,
# FALSE for the others.
covered = NA

# Coverage: the fraction of samples whose interval contains the shape.
mean(covered)
```

3. Set seed 802 and repeat questions 1 and 2 with hypothetical samples of 150 trees from
   the same model: call `simulate_gamma_samples()` with `n_obs = 150`, store the result in
   `trees_150`, and use `trees_150` in place of `trees_31` in the chunk of question 2. How
   do the bias and the coverage change, and why?
4. Why do these results only approximate the behaviour of the estimators and the interval
   for the real trees?
